ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Colorectal adenocarcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumour of the colon or rectum, arising from dysplastic adenomas. It is staged by depth of invasion and nodal spread, which drive prognosis and treatment.

sections.p: A malignant gland‑forming tumour of the colorectal mucosa, usually arising from adenomatous polyps. Diagnosis requires histology from biopsy or resection, with immunohistochemistry confirming adenocarcinoma.
b: Histology shows glandular structures with nuclear atypia and invasion of submucosa

t.b: Detects mucosal lesions and obtains tissue for histology; positive finding confirms tumour
Assesses local extension and distant metastasis; abnormal nodes or masses suggest advanced disease
Elevated levels support diagnosis and monitor recurrence; normal CEA does not exclude cancer

sections.p: TNM staging is used: T describes depth of tumour invasion, N indicates lymph node involvement, M denotes distant metastasis. Stage I–IV guides treatment and prognosis.

t.b: Provides T and N stages; T4 or N+ indicates poorer prognosis
Detects occult metastases; positive findings upgrade to stage IV

sections.p: The adenoma‑carcinoma sequence is the main pathway, driven by genetic mutations (APC, KRAS, p53). Risk factors include age, diet, smoking, alcohol, obesity, IBD, and inherited syndromes.
b: APC mutation leads to adenoma formation

t.b: Suggests FAP or HNPCC; prompts genetic testing
Increases risk of dysplasia; surveillance colonoscopy recommended

sections.p: Symptoms evolve gradually: altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, anemia, weight loss, abdominal pain, and sometimes obstruction or perforation.

t.b: Low Hb and ferritin suggest chronic bleeding from tumour

sections.p: A combination of endoscopy, imaging, and laboratory tests establishes diagnosis, staging, and guides therapy.

t.b: Assesses T stage when tumour is near the rectum; helps plan surgery
Evaluates mesorectal fascia involvement in rectal cancer

sections.p: Urgent signs include severe bleeding, obstruction, perforation, or rapid weight loss. Complications can be local (obstruction) or systemic (metastasis).
b: Large rectal bleeding may require transfusion

t.b: Detects perforation if free air is seen

sections.p: Treatment follows the TNM stage: surgery for localized disease, chemotherapy for node‑positive or metastatic disease, and radiotherapy for rectal tumours.
b: Surgery removes tumour and involved nodes

t.b: Targets rapidly dividing cells; chosen for stage III and IV
Oral alternative to 5‑FU; similar efficacy but different toxicity profile

sections.p: Regular surveillance colonoscopy after resection detects recurrence or new adenomas. Lifestyle changes reduce risk.

t.b: Detects metachronous lesions; early removal improves outcomes

sections.p: Inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulitis, and benign polyps can mimic cancer symptoms.
b: IBD flare may cause bleeding and pain

t.b: Differentiates malignant glands from inflammatory changes

sections.p: Normal CEA does not rule out cancer; early tumours may not elevate it. Small polyps may be missed on colonoscopy if inadequate bowel prep.

t.b: If symptoms persist despite negative initial study

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain suggesting obstruction or perforation
Rapid weight loss or new anemia

faq.q: What is the most important prognostic factor in colorectal cancer?
faq.a: Depth of tumour invasion (T stage) and presence of lymph node metastases (N stage).
Regular screening colonoscopy and a diet low in red meat, high in fibre, and maintaining a healthy weight reduce risk.

faq.q: Why is CEA not always reliable?
faq.a: Early tumours may not produce enough antigen; some benign conditions can raise CEA, so it is adjunctive, not definitive.

exam: Explain how the adenoma‑carcinoma sequence leads to colorectal cancer and why APC mutation is central.
Describe the TNM staging system and its impact on treatment decisions.
Outline the key investigations for a patient with suspected colorectal cancer and interpret a normal versus abnormal CEA level.
